text:
With regards to meaning and purpose, I feel like understanding reality in the context of a video game can be useful to some limited extent. In a video game you know (I would hope) what the purpose of the video game is, you will usually find out the bigger picture (or get told straight away) and discover the details of the game (more so as you play it). Given this, you can apply logic/etc/whatever to how YOU want to play the game.

Obviously life is not exactly like a video game, there is (as far as I'm aware) no consciousness inside a video game, among many other dissimilarities. But real life is a bit like being thrown into a video game whereby you don't choose your character. Like all characters (I assume) you start off mostly ignorant. You don't choose the point in time/history you are in, etc, etc.

You don't know the rules of the video game (laws of nature, etc), you don't KNOW the bigger picture (including whether the 'video game' has a creator or not, etc). You are (imo) both individually and collectively unlikely to 'figure out' the 'video game' of life during your/our life time. With the intergenerational transfer and development/recording of 'knowledge' hopefully our ignorance decreases over time.

And so my point being, it's no wonder people struggle. Beliefs about this 'video game' that help us know how to orient our character within the video game (e.g. the bigger picture, the details, who our character is, etc, etc) are what enables us (imo) to have meaning, purpose, satisfaction, etc, in life.

As I said, video games have no consciousness, reality is not a video game. Because consciousness exists (including suffering), morality is a real concept and something worth pursuing/holding on to. But my point is, looking at reality, to some extent, as like being thrown into a strange video game where we don't even know if it's a video game or not is imo conceptually helpful to benefiting people in life (regarding how to orient themselves, etc).

In my opinion meaning is relational. For example, a tree can be meaningful to various beings in various contexts. E.g. animals may use it for shelter, a source of food (insects hiding within), nest potential, etc. A human may see it meaningful as a source of firewood, a means to build something like a wooden toy for their child, shelter from the weather, etc.

I wish I had this view/mindset in my late teens/early 20s. I would have told myself to investigate reality, arrive at high level beliefs about the bigger picture (existential beliefs, beliefs about existence), the details (how reality works) and my character (who am I?), etc. Once I've established enough of these related beliefs I will (I think) find meaning, find purpose and begin to actually start my life.

Note: this doesn't assume a one size fits all answer. Some will say the bigger picture is a particular kind of God and so that will affect how they interact with/view the 'video game' of life.'. Also, in my opinion, some aspect (perhaps a lot) of life are speculative and given the diversity of perspectives/points of view, variety of orientation would exist even without this level of speculation.

Just as there are no rights without an equivalent responsibility, in a democracy, there is no responsibility without an equivalent right.

Responsibility means acting in recognition of the personhood of the other person, the full citizen. That is, of recognising their fundamental right to be treated equally in that citizenship. The discourse on rights is just an elaboration of the detail of that recognition.

Power is not necessarily responsibility.  Power is very often exercised disregarding the personhood of the other. This occurs in societies which have only a weak or merely formal understanding of citizenship.

It is for this reason that Nazism and Stalinism are seen as some of the most egregious failures of the state and why they gave rise to the post 2ww UN Universal Declaration of Human Rights and the many international treaties on rights that define democratic societies.

So Peterson's dismissive comments on the issue of rights are both misplaced but also, IMO, are irresponsible. 

To talk of rights and responsibilities is to look at the same issue of the full recognition of the human person from different angles.

To dismiss this discourse is to dismantle the basic theory of liberal democracy.

Responsibility without rights has a name, China. Be careful what you wish for.

Jordan Peterson’s 12 rules for life - an appraisal.

*Stand up straight with your shoulders straight.* Unless you’re a peeping Tom and need to keep below that wall, otherwise that gorgeous, undressing next-door neighbour may spot you.
*Treat yourself like someone you are responsible for helping.* In other words, pick up your own smelly socks, don’t litter, and make your own fucking bed!

*Compare yourself to who you were yesterday, not the useless person you are today.* This one totally contradicts the whole idea of self-improvement, for if I’m more useless today than I was yesterday, why am I even trying to self-improve?!
*Do not let your children do anything that makes you dislike them.* Well, this assumes that you’re such an insane parental control freak with such a fascistic sense of keeping another in order that it’s not even worth considering, if only to save your own soul. Jordan Peterson‘s 12 *more* (God help us all!) rules for life - an appraisal.

*Work as hard as you possibly can on at least one thing and see what happens.* Well, since the age of about 13 I’ve been actively fulfilling this injunction and it’s nearly fallen off.😳
*Try to make one room in your home as beautiful as possible.* Can we agree on a corner of one room? A whole room just sounds extravagant and, frankly, a waste of my time when I’ve got rule 7 to be getting on with.😳
*If old memories still upset you, write them down carefully and completely.*  Yes, they do. However, not sure writing them down will help. Can I not just do the more obvious, sensible thing and, er, like, well, forget them?

From high school till the time I was 21 I had a hard time maintaining a job I thought I “liked”. Most was chasing status so others could be impressed with me but I’d get this “high status” job and would only like a few months till satisfaction of everyone being impressed with me went away. And when I’d quit this job because of the lost connection I had going into the job I’d fall into a deep depression, nihilistic, did nothing but bullshit in my room for months and months because of the overwhelming feeling of saturation that was in area of work.. I’d be become almost intimidated like I couldn’t ever be that guy. And this cycle would repeat so I’d stay in my room, but playing the game GTA years later now that I was older, I’d do all these “missions” and was chasing this status in the game of being a multimillionaire and having and doing whatever the hell I wanted brought one of the most life changing analogies to come into my head. And I thought “why do I spend all this time doing these missions just have and do whatever and not doing it for myself in this reality” i was beginning to change how saw an approach to life and began to treat myself like a character in a game and whatever mission I have to do in the real life I’ll do to get to that point in hopefully real life. This approach changed a lot for me and I got a job and eventually moved out with my girl friend. We lived there for awhile but things got ugly with room mates so we had to leave. The separation of feeling like I was the support, or that I was responsible for taking care of us now that we back to our own parents houses, left me with constant anxiety attacks and this feeling panic for 10 days straight, I’d begin to freak out more not realizing the source of why I was beginning to go down a steep spiral again. 
Still 21 years old, I’m back on feet after almost letting myself slip into my parents basement forever, I have this sense of urgency to have our own place again.

DO THE HARD WORK, ESPECIALLY WHEN YOU DON'T FEEL LIKE IT

I am a therapist. Here are my thoughts on the issue: I think there are definitely cases where individual therapists overly focus on making their clients feel "heard and loved". Building rapport is essential to successful therapy, though I wouldn't say that I was taught to make my clients feel "heard and loved", more that they need to feel "understood" and feel that you're on their side and invested in their well being. I was also taught, by a female psychologist no less, that men and women process their emotions differently, with men being more likely to lash out and become outwardly destructive, while women were more likely to turn inward. Male depression was more likely to present as outward anger while women were more likely to develop negative feelings towards themselves. Of course, men are perfectly capable of turning inward and women can definitely lash out as well. These are just tendencies.

When it comes to general practices and trends in therapy, I would guess that the source of this male dissatisfaction with therapy may be because the field has become so female dominant lately. With more and more women, female perspectives may come to dominate therapeutic approaches without adequately accounting for male needs.

I would also say that men are more often focused on "solving" their problems. I usually find a lot of the male-generated discourse about men and boys being oppressed in modern society pretty sensationalist, but the two therapists I saw (both of whom were women) were actually like actively unhelpful. I am (or was, at this point) a collegiate varsity athlete who has been struggling with depression and disordered eating, as well as just a general dissatisfaction with life and lack of excitement. I felt like a lot of the things I was struggling with were of a very masculine nature, in the sense that I felt meaningless and lacking direction/fulfillment. I wasn't really struggling with not feeling loved or being emotionally disconnected from my peers or anything like that. Both therapists really infantilized me and seemed to simply be incapable of understanding that a masculine identity was not inherently toxic. So many times it felt like they were trying to persuade me to try acting less like a man, and they consistently seemed to brush me off when I tried to get help with the real issues I felt like I was struggling with.

It's just a fact that overall culture has feminized (or at least de-masculinized) in the past few decades. In many ways, this is a good thing, as its opening up more opportunities for women and giving men some much-needed perspective. However, it is also a fact that modern western societies simply have less room for masculine people and that the personality traits most prized and rewarded are traditionally feminine ones, as seen in massive increase in the size of the services at the expense of manufacturing/blue collar jobs. Hopefully this is just a case of the pendulum swinging too far and out of this people have more nuanced perspectives on what it means to be a man and what it means to be a women, as I feel like masculine and feminine identities have both been severely disrupted and thrown out of wack by recent events.

When I was a teenager, I was picked on relentlessly. Not physically (I could have dealt with that), but mentally and emotionally. I had one friend, but he was grades older than me, he couldn't help me. No adult would listen when I had a problem because the teachers wouldn't care if I was on the verge of crying or so full of hate I wanted to kill someone (not exaggerating in the least) because I wasn't physically being abused.
Eventually, I saw a therapist, and, for the first few weeks, it did nothing but help me vent. They prescribed pills, but I hated taking pills so most of the time, I didn't actually take them. However, after a while, they helped me reach an epiphany that, truth be told, was pretty obvious, but this helped me internalize it. Soon after, I stopped seeing the therapist, and my parent's remarked how well the medication worked. The medication I didn't take.
And, here's the thing. The therapist did indeed help my emotions even out just because I had nobody to vent them to, or was willing to listen at all. That did help, but it was the active revelation about standing up for myself and gatekeeping who I should even listen to that actually made a difference. I was so desperate for friends and acceptance that I was letting every piece of shit in. Once I internalized that that was the problem, I took away the power the others had over me, and, even though I was still mostly alone, I was alone with the walls necessary to keep the assholes out.
All I needed was (other than a social climate that didn't resemble an ocean tank filled with sharks and leeches) the realization that I was in control of more than I thought. I couldn't control them, but, at the same time, they couldn't control me. I controlled me. That little bit was enough, and, honestly, probably saved the lives of some people.

text:
I'm currently in training to be a therapist, so you could say this interview has come about at an interesting time where I can look at the models we use and see the flaws and usefulness of them. It's also worth noting the interviewee specifically talking about brain patterns and studies, which leans very specifically towards a more narrow field of therapy which again is great if you want to generalize about 'all' men as statistics, but people are pretty individual when it comes down to a one to one basis. 2 men might do the same thing but have entirely different motivations and thoughts behind why they are doing it. The action doesn't make them men just because they are both men who did it and a 3rd man who doesn't do that action isn't any less a man for not doing it?... a vague metaphor but it feels relevant to mention.

I think one of the key things he mentions here is actually very early on where he speaks about men 'wanting' a solution, which is also quite a broad assumption as I have therapy and have found the deeper learning into my behavior's (conscious and subconscious) very handy in understanding my thoughts and behavior's and the impact on me and others around me it has. Yes there is the solution in understanding but it's not necessarily as clear cut as a cure or fix as he seems to suggest there 'should' be. There is also a dependency on the client bringing everything they have to the session (mentally speaking). Some don't want you to explore, or pry, uncover. A lot of depressed people feel unheard to the point of pushing even caring people away, it's what helps facilitate their mindset and provides them a comfort in 'knowing' their own truths whilst isolated. Therapy isn't about giving you the answer you want and you leaving the session 100% fixed. There also isn't a 'one size fits all'. 

Therapy is about the learning, the working through and understanding of what exists. There are sure enough some styles which address maladaptive behavior's and how to address them and work on them, but they have to be identified by the client (in CBT) but other forms of therapy mainly look into the learning and understanding of the individual, it doesn't necessarily come about with a mission to 'cure' or a 'solution', but more a mission to understand, and on that note, is likely why there are some men who I can see the in the comments section for example, who don't get the experience they were looking for but also perhaps didn't have the right kind of therapy they needed - most people don't know that different therapists can specialize in different styles for example.

I'm glad its a topic people are talking about. I hope it brings more men into the therapy setting as both therapists and clients alike, and I hope it encourages men to be more vocal on how they feel, because that all leads to the therapy being more effective if the therapist understands fully what you are looking to achieve.
